A company funded specifically for 'NORTHCOM and Platform One' application security whose site now names zero accreditation concepts — no ATO, RMF, STIG, IL5, Iron Bank, FedRAMP, or CMMC — and whose Industries menu reads 'Critical Infrastructure, Finance, Healthcare, Technology' with no defense vertical at all → deployment_awareness_absence

blind_spots.blind_spot: The Air Force money bought a NORTHCOM/Platform One capability, and no part of the current product has a path back onto a DoD endpoint
blind_spots.operator_reality: To run on a government host the agent needs an ATO on that enclave, STIG-compliant configuration, and — if it ships the way Platform One ships things — a hardened container in Iron Bank with continuous vulnerability scanning and a signed SBOM. That work is 9-18 months and has to be funded by someone. Right now defense is not even one of the four industries listed in their own navigation, which means the $750K Phase II produced a commercial product and an unclaimed transition.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The commercial anti-ransomware market pulled hard and paid immediately (Veeam integration, macOS support, Microsoft for Startups); the accreditation work pays nothing until it is finished, so it lost every prioritization argument.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Homogeneous software applications employed throughout NORTHCOM and Platform One pose a huge opportunity for adversaries to scale exploits within the defense ecosystem.

blind_spots.blind_spot: Concealment as a product mechanic collides with the government's own audit and incident-response requirements
blind_spots.operator_reality: 'Stealth directories' hide files from an attacker — and from the defender's tooling too. On a DoD endpoint, host-based security, asset inventory, and DFIR all require that the filesystem be enumerable and auditable by the government's own stack; an incident responder who cannot see a directory has an audit finding, not a feature. Fielding means deconflicting moving-target defense with ESS/HBSS agents, endpoint logging into the government SIEM, and forensic imaging procedures. That negotiation with the accreditor is the actual deployment work, and it is not a settings toggle.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: In a commercial environment the CISO owns both the concealment tool and the audit requirement, so the conflict is resolved in a meeting. In DoD the accreditor is a different authority with a veto and no incentive to accommodate.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Hide critical files from an attacker with stealth directories so they are never found or affected.

blind_spots.blind_spot: Foreign-distributed engineering on a privileged endpoint agent bound for defense hosts
blind_spots.operator_reality: An agent with deep filesystem privilege on a government endpoint gets scrutinized for supply-chain provenance: who commits to it, where it is built, whether CUI touched a non-compliant system, and whether non-US persons had access to the technical data. A workforce spread across the US, Argentina, and Singapore turns CMMC/NIST 800-171 and a software provenance review into a structural problem rather than a paperwork exercise — and it is the kind of finding that arrives after the technical evaluation is already won.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The distributed team is a cost and hiring advantage that has never cost them a commercial deal; the constraint only exists on the government side of the house they stopped selling to.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Its workforce is distributed across United States, Argentina, and Singapore.

opener_hook: Arms Cyber's 2022 Air Force Phase II was written for NORTHCOM and Platform One application security, and today armscyber.com lists four industries — Critical Infrastructure, Finance, Healthcare, Technology — with no defense vertical and no mention of ATO, STIG, or Iron Bank anywhere on the site.
what_they_do: Sells an endpoint anti-ransomware platform that uses moving-target defense — hiding files in stealth directories, adapting to anomalous behavior, and restoring from concealed backups.
